$comment: The claims ledger. Every sentence that appears in the README, the demo
script, or on screen has a row here, and `scripts/verify.ts` turns each row
into an assertion that fails the run when it stops being true.
Two fields carry the weight, and they are deliberately separate:
proof.runsAgainst — WHAT THAT PROOF RUNS AGAINST
The second field exists because four times in this build a green check
certified behaviour the real system did not exhibit, and every time the
reason was the same: the assertion was sound and the thing it ran against
was a mock. `holdsNoFunds()` passed in the suite while the deployed registry
held 0.24 tUSDC, because the mock refunded escrow synchronously and the
venue does not. So a claim whose only runsAgainst is `mock` is capped at
SUITE-ONLY no matter how many tests back it.
`provenance` records what the evidence was taken FROM. verify.ts recomputes
the deployed code hash and, when it has moved, reports the claim AMBER
rather than green — a measurement that outlives its build is how 789 gas
and a batch cap of 24 both nearly reached a README.

deployed.$comment: The handler was redeployed on 5 Sep to add the H1 instrumentation. The previous one (0xDED8c0bE939cCe19f27176E5F33deA7b2A4DE35C) is drained and dead; nothing should reference it.

statuses.LIVE-ASSERTED: verify.ts asserts it against deployed contracts on the real network
statuses.LIVE-PROVEN: a real transaction on the explorer is the evidence
statuses.SUITE-ONLY: backed by unit tests against mocks; NOT proof about the venue
statuses.MEASURED: a number read from receipts or balance deltas on the deployed build
statuses.UNBACKED: stated nowhere yet, because nothing currently proves it

claims.claim: The registry holds no funds. Every unit of collateral in it is owed to a named party.

proof.runsAgainst: the deployed registry on Somnia Shannon — not a mock

claims.history: This was green in the unit suite while the deployed registry held 0.24 tUSDC. The mock refunded escrow synchronously; the venue does not. Fixed with a per-mandate refundClaim and a permissionless sweepRefunds, and the assertion moved on-chain.

claims.claim: Refunded escrow is attributed to the mandate that reserved it, never pooled.
claims.history: A pooled sweep once paid a 3-mandate settlement out of 12 unrelated mandates' escrow.

claims.claim: Non-upgradeable. No proxy, no admin key, no owner role, no pause.

proof.assertion: A three-link chain, in this order. Each link is checkable on its own and the conclusion needs all three.
proof.runsAgainst: the deployed registry's runtime bytecode and storage, plus the solc artifact those bytes were compiled from
chain: 1. DEPLOYED == ARTIFACT. eth_getCode(registry), with immutable slots masked and solc's CBOR metadata trailer stripped, is byte-for-byte equal to contracts/out/MandateRegistry.sol/MandateRegistry.json deployedBytecode. Only the 32-byte IPFS metadata hash differs, and that changes when a COMMENT changes - source drift, not semantic drift.

2. ARTIFACT HAS NO UPGRADE PATH. solc's own instruction listing (evm.legacyAssembly, emitted via extra_output in foundry.toml) reports 0 DELEGATECALL and 0 SELFDESTRUCT across 5,802 runtime instructions, and its methodIdentifiers table contains none of owner/admin/pause/unpause/upgradeTo/upgradeToAndCall/transferOwnership/withdraw/setOwner/initialize among 30 entry points.
3. STORAGE IS NOT A PROXY. eth_getStorageAt on all three EIP-1967 slots (implementation, admin, beacon) returns zero.
Link 1 is what makes link 2 a statement about the DEPLOYMENT rather than about a local file. Without it, the compiler listing describes a program that may not be the one on chain.

claims.history: Was SUITE-ONLY: the source said immutable and the tests never checked the deployed artifact. The first live version of this check used a LINEAR DISASSEMBLY of the deployed bytes and reported 'DELEGATECALL opcode present in registry runtime' at offset 8557. `cast disassemble` independently agreed. Both were wrong: solc appends data blobs after the code, a linear scan desyncs inside them and starts reading operands as opcodes, and offset 8557 is the middle of a 32-byte constant (2335ccf1...d302). This is recorded because a judge who knows disassembly will run the same scan, get the same false positive, and the answer should be readable here without re-deriving it. Never assert an opcode's absence from a linear scan of EVM bytecode; ask the compiler that emitted it.

provenance.requires: foundry.toml extra_output = ["evm.legacyAssembly"]; verify.ts REFUSES to fall back to a linear disassembly if the artifact lacks it

claims.claim: A validator invocation cannot be forged, by a competitor or by us.

proof.assertion: Calling onEvent on the DEPLOYED handler from an ordinary EOA reverts. Only 0x0100 passes the check in SomniaEventHandler.onEvent.
proof.runsAgainst: the deployed handler, via eth_call from a funded stranger key

claims.history: Was SOURCE-READABLE only — true of the library, unproven of our deployment.

claims.claim: The delegate cannot exceed the per-order cap, the cumulative budget, the market list, or the expiry, and cannot revoke or redirect funds.

proof.assertion: 41 unit tests (28 enforcement + 13 revocation) AND, on the deployed registry, each of the six named errors is provoked from a real key and the raw eth_call revert data decodes to that exact selector.
proof.runsAgainst: unit tests run against mocks; the six refusals run against the DEPLOYED registry — which is the half that counts

claims.history: A reentrancy test asserted a guard it never triggered, because the mock token had no callback. The rule that came out of it: an assertion is only as strong as the fidelity of what it runs against.

claims.claim: Deleting the Deadhand handler and its subscription leaves a fully working app. The handler is one caller among several, never the source of truth.

proof.assertion: A stranger key — not the delegator, not the delegate, not the handler — calls settleFinalizedMarket directly and it succeeds.
proof.runsAgainst: the deployed registry, with the handler unsubscribed and not in the call path

claims.history: An earlier delete-test passed vacuously: it used a simulated orderId, so settle was a silent no-op that still returned status=success.

claims.claim: When a market resolves, validators invoke the handler and it settles every affected mandate in that block - releasing exposure, revoking breachers, and sweeping payouts to the delegator, who never traded. Measured at 3, 8 and 12 mandates in single invocations on the deployed bytecode.

proof.assertion: A Deadhand event from a real validator invocation, with processed == the number of mandates seeded and drained == true.
proof.runsAgainst: the CURRENT deployed handler bytecode, invoked by validators on a real MarketFinalized

claims.history: The previous evidence was on a superseded handler deployment whose marketsSettled counter reads 0 — i.e. it never settled anything at this address. Re-proven on the current build.

claims.claim: The handler settles a bounded batch of 17 mandates, sized from a fit on the deployed bytecode and corroborated by an out-of-gas ceiling observed at 32.
appearsIn: answer to: how does this scale

proof.assertion: batchCap on the deployed handler EQUALS floor(0.5 x where the shipped 8,000,000 gasLimit binds), computed from an ordinary-least-squares fit over the points in .measurements/deadhand-fit.json that were measured on the deployed code hash. verify.ts asserts the equality, not merely that a fit exists.
proof.runsAgainst: gasUsed read from Deadhand events emitted by REAL validator invocations on the current bytecode, at two batch sizes, plus a third invocation at n=32 that ran OUT OF GAS and bounds the line from above

claims.history: Shipped as 24 from a fit taken on handler 0xDED8c0bE..., whose marketsSettled counter reads 0 - it never settled anything at that address. Also briefly stood at 32 while a measurement run was in flight, and verify.ts passed it green because the check asserted that measurement points EXISTED but not that the deployed cap followed from them. That hole is closed. | 8 Sep: re-fitted on 0x6ec80e8a after the registry redeploy. n=3 1,550,679 and n=12 3,302,336 give ~966,795 fixed + ~194,628 per mandate, binding at 35 and shipping at 17. A run at n=32 was DELIVERED and FAILED at the 8,000,000 limit (DeadhandFailed, pendingSettlement stayed 32), so the real cost there exceeds ~7.89M against a predicted 7.19M - the two-point line under-predicts at high n by at least 10%, the same direction as the +5.8% seen on the previous bytecode. Taking the ceiling as the slope puts binding at ~32, which is why 17 keeps its 50% headroom rather than being raised.
claims.caveat: RESOLVED. The two-point fit rested on one point that was the handler's first-ever settle, which deflated the slope - the dangerous direction. The n=32 point corrects it: marginal rises from 216,807 to 233,279 (+7.6%), and the two-point fit under-predicted the real n=32 cost by 5.8% (7,637,929 predicted vs 8,082,346 measured). The 50% headroom absorbed the error and the cap is unchanged at 13.
points: n=3   1,350,525 gas  (handler's first-ever settle; pays zero->nonzero counter writes)
n=32  8,082,346 gas  (40 reservations open, so the cap clipped it: processed=32, drained=false)

fit.allThreePoints: fixed ~590,175 gas + marginal ~233,279 gas/mandate; binds at ~26; cap 13
fit.warmOnly_excludingFirstEver: fixed ~433,450 gas + marginal ~239,028 gas/mandate; binds at ~26; cap 13
fit.note: Both give 13, which is why the caveat below is now closed rather than merely tolerated.

claims.whyTheCapMatters: Not theoretical. The n=32 settle consumed 8,082,346 gas. Under the SHIPPED 8,000,000 subscription gasLimit that batch would have run out of gas and settled nothing - it only completed because the measurement run armed at 10,000,000. A cap above ~26 is not a conservative choice, it is a broken one.

claims.claim: Ignoring a finalization that is not ours costs 0.00174709 STT per invocation (~256,924 gas at the observed 6.8 gwei), deterministic across invocations.

proof.assertion: Balance delta over a window in which the handler had ZERO mandates, so every invocation took the skip path and nothing else. 6 pure skips, no settles mixed in. The STT figure is measured; the gas figure is derived from it and depends on the assumed effective price.
proof.runsAgainst: receipts of live validator invocations against the deployed handler — not a balance delta divided by a count

claims.caveat: Quotable ONLY with the armed cost attached: ~15.1 STT/day at one finalization per 10s. 'We subscribe to everything and pay a rounding error' is FALSE and must not be said. The argument that survives is the shape, not the price: one subscription regardless of how many delegations exist, against a per-user-per-order model that scales with users x orders.
claims.history: RETRACTED: 0.00044017 STT / ~64,700 gas. That figure does not reproduce on this build, and the ~28,000 gas of H1 instrumentation added since does not explain a 4.5x gap. Retracted as unexplained rather than re-derived — inventing an explanation is how the previous three wrong numbers survived. Also retracted: 789 gas (probe handler), and 78,100 / ~339,000 (both divided out of MIXED windows and disagreeing by 4x).
claims.alsoEstablished: Charging is on gas USED, not gasLimit: the identical figure came back to the wei at gasLimit 3,000,000 and 8,000,000 — same call, one variable changed. And pendingSettlement is O(1), so the skip cost does not grow with the mandate count.
claims.note: Measured twice, 20 minutes apart, on the same bytecode: 0.00174709 STT per skip both times, identical to the wei. The receipts above are from the second run - the first captured none, because this RPC serves 1000 blocks (~100s) and the window had already scrolled past by the time anyone went looking. measure-skip.ts now collects them while they are still readable.

claims.claim: One subscription serves every delegation. dreamDEX's SpotStopOrderRegistry funds one per user per order.

proof.assertion: The handler has exactly one subscriptionId, and the settle it performs covers every mandate on the resolved market regardless of how many delegators are involved. subscribeTo is not payable and takes no per-user argument.
proof.runsAgainst: the deployed handler's ABI and its subscriptionId storage slot

claims.claim: No indexer, no REST API, no third-party service sits on the path between opening the app and placing an order.

proof.assertion: NEGATIVE TEST. No shipped module references an indexer or REST host; market discovery reads MarketCreated logs straight from the binaryModule singleton and still returns markets. Pointed at a dead RPC, discovery THROWS rather than returning an empty list.
proof.runsAgainst: the shipped source of apps/web and packages/leash-ec, plus a live discovery run and a deliberately unroutable RPC

claims.history: The indexer went down mid-build and every SDK discovery path went through it. Chain-only discovery was written that day.

claims.claim: Every mandate limit and the held-by-registry figure are read from the contract. Nothing that looks like a mandate limit is decorative.

proof.assertion: NEGATIVE TEST. readHeld() against an unroutable RPC returns the em dash and read=false, never '0.00'. The monitor and delegate envelopes render their own age from chainAt and say so when a poll has failed. The price chart is labelled indicative.
proof.runsAgainst: the SHIPPED function apps/web/src/held.ts, called with a dead client — not a re-implementation of it in a test

claims.history: The chart ships under an explicit override of the read-only-mirror rule. The hard line attached to that override is this claim, which is why it gets a negative test rather than an inspection.

claims.claim: The delegate places a real Event Contract order that the venue accepts, drawing on an allowance the delegator can revoke at any moment. The principal is pulled just-in-time and swept back in the same transaction; the delegator has signed nothing but an ERC-20 approve.

proof.assertion: BinaryOrderPlaced in the receipt of a placeForDelegator transaction sent by the delegate key, with the order id read from topics[1] of that log.
proof.runsAgainst: live dreamDEX binary pools on Somnia Shannon, 14 rehearsal runs

claims.caveat: A FILL IS NOT PROMISED and must not be scripted. Binary books are quote-only: 161 orders on binary pools produced 1 fill in ~100s, while 35 fills happened on spot/perp in the same window. Across 14 rehearsals, 1 filled and 13 rested. The second evidence hash is the one that filled; the first is the ordinary case. Beat 2 proves the authorization and just-in-time custody path, which is ours, not the presence of a counterparty, which is not.

claims.claim: The delegate's attempt to move funds reverts on our own authorization check, not on an incidental 'nothing to withdraw'.

proof.assertion: The registry exposes no withdraw function at all — no selector to call. revoke() from the delegate key MINES AND REVERTS with NotDelegator: a real transaction with status 0 on the explorer, not a simulation and not a frontend message. 14/14 rehearsals.
proof.runsAgainst: the deployed registry, called from the real delegate key

claims.history: An error decoder once matched the SENDER ADDRESS with a regex and reported it as a revert selector. Selectors are decoded from raw return data, never pattern-matched out of a message string.

claims.claim: Event Contracts expose no per-user authorization surface. placeBinaryOrderFor is gated by OnlyApprovedContracts() and rejects even the owner acting for itself, so no EOA can ever be granted pool-level authority.

proof.assertion: PROBE A. Identical call, one variable changed, raw eth_call return data, three senders. All three revert with 0x3fb0ba2e including the owner for itself, while the same order via placeBinaryOrder(self) passes authorization and fails on allowance.
proof.runsAgainst: the live binary pool implementation resolved through its beacon — not ec-core's bundled address, which is stale

openHypotheses.question: A previous handler deployment recorded 474 invocations and zero settles. Was our market's MarketFinalized never delivered (H1a), or delivered and skipped by the pendingSettlement == 0 path (H1b)?
openHypotheses.status: DISTINGUISHABLE — and not reproduced on the current build
openHypotheses.distinguishingTest: seen[marketId] on the deployed handler. Zero after a finalization we watched for is H1a; non-zero with no settle is H1b.
openHypotheses.firstResult: Two runs, 5 Sep: seen[marketId] == 1 both times and both settled. Neither branch fired. That does not retire H1 - it means the instrumentation now answers the question the next time it happens, which is the point.
openHypotheses.note: The two were indistinguishable precisely because the emit that separated them had been trimmed for gas.

knownLimitations.severity: HIGH in a multi-delegator deployment; not triggered in this build's own runs
knownLimitations.what: MandateRegistry._sweep keeps only `totalOwed`, not `totalOwed + totalRefundClaim`. Collateral that has been booked as delegator A's refundClaim can therefore be swept to delegator B by B's next placeForDelegator, because _sweep sends `balance - totalOwed` to whichever delegator's order is executing.
knownLimitations.observed: Directly: 1.98 tUSDC returned to the registry from cancelExpiredOrders, then vanished while refundClaim still read 1.98. Re-run with nothing racing it, the correct path paid the delegator in full and cleared the claim.
knownLimitations.whyTheInvariantStillPasses: holdsNoFunds() asserts balance <= totalOwed + totalRefundClaim. Sweeping money OUT only lowers the balance, so the invariant holds — vacuously. It proves we hold nothing unattributed; it does not prove every attributed claim is backed by collateral we still hold. That is a second invariant this contract does not assert.
knownLimitations.blastRadius: Requires A's escrow to be sitting in the registry when B places an order. Escrow only arrives when someone explicitly calls cancelExpiredOrders or redeem on the venue, so the window is narrow in practice and did not occur across the rehearsal set, where every mandate shares one delegator.
knownLimitations.fix: One line: `uint256 keep = totalOwed + totalRefundClaim;`. The contract is IMMUTABLE by design, so applying it means redeploying the registry AND the handler (its `registry` pointer is immutable), which invalidates every evidence hash and the batch-cap fit's code hash.
knownLimitations.status: DISCLOSED, NOT FIXED. Recorded rather than quietly left in place.

knownLimitations.severity: affects the demo narrative, not custody
knownLimitations.what: Settlement releases exposure and books a refundClaim, but the venue does not push the collateral back. Someone must call cancelExpiredOrders (or redeem) on the pool first; sweepRefunds then pays the delegator.
knownLimitations.observed: totalRefundClaim reached 11.42 tUSDC with a registry balance of 0 across the measurement and rehearsal runs.
knownLimitations.mitigation: Both legs are PERMISSIONLESS and were both executed from a stranger key, so the delegator never depends on us being online. The handler does not do it in-callback.
knownLimitations.consequence: Beat 3's in-block action is settle + revoke + book. The payout is a second, permissionless step. Do not narrate it as money moving in the same block.
